stages.title: Backward vertical integration: gains and risks
stages.sub: Weigh up what a business gains and risks when it buys its own supplier.

steps.q: A coffee shop chain used to buy its beans from an independent farm. It then buys that farm outright. Whose job is growing and grading the beans now?
steps.hint: The farm is no longer a separate outside business once it is bought.

steps.q: Before, a rival supplier sometimes ran out of beans or sent a poor batch. Now the chain owns that stage itself. Does it have more say over what beans it gets and when?
steps.right: Yes, it now controls that directly
steps.wrong: No, it has no more say than before
steps.hint: The growing stage is now run by the chain's own managers, not an outside firm.
steps.pre: Owning that stage lets the firm

steps.q: Before buying the farm, the chain paid a price that included the farm's own profit on top of its costs. After buying the farm, does the chain still have to pay that extra profit to a separate owner?
steps.right: No, that extra profit is no longer paid out
steps.wrong: Yes, it still pays that same extra amount
steps.hint: The farm's profit used to go to a separate owner. Where does it go now that the chain owns the farm?

steps.q: The coffee chain's managers have spent years running cafes, not farms. Once they own that stage, will they automatically be as skilled at growing coffee as the farmers were?
steps.right: No, they lack that specific know-how
steps.wrong: Yes, running any business is the same skill
steps.hint: Growing crops well needs different knowledge from running a cafe. Does owning the stage hand over that knowledge too?
